exceptions.rationale: emlkit decodes Base64 data after padding as a further segment (cte.base64_data_after_padding, a deliberate choice so a scanner sees what a permissive client shows): "hihi". Python's non-strict fallback misdecodes the second group into "hi\x1a\x1a".

emlkit reads the misspelled Content-Transfer-Encoding 'quoted_printable' as quoted-printable (cte.invalid_token) and decodes '=E2=82=AC' to the euro sign, 37 bytes; Python does not recognize the value and delivers the 43 encoded bytes, which no mail client shows.
emlkit reads 'base-64' as base64 (cte.invalid_token): its body is the 46 bytes of HTML the text decodes to. Python does not recognize the value and delivers the 64 bytes of base64 text.

The bytes differ in one place, 'busin=   \r\ness': emlkit deletes the spaces after the '=' at the end of the line as transport padding (RFC 2045 section 6.7, rule 3), which leaves a soft line break, and gives "business", 223 bytes (cte.qp_invalid_soft_break); Python's binascii.a2b_qp keeps '=   \r\n' as text, 229 bytes. The rest of the damage, a soft break ended by a bare LF and the escape '=E2=8=' split by a soft break, decodes the same on both sides.
emlkit reads the Content-Transfer-Encoding value '"BASE64"; x=1' as base64 (cte.invalid_token) and decodes the body; Python does not recognize the value and keeps the encoded text.

emlkit decodes the base64 a message/rfc822 part declares before reading the message it carries (message.illegal_transfer_encoding); Python parses the encoded text itself as the embedded message, which then has no header and a body of base64.

emlkit keeps a colonless line apart as an orphan record and goes on reading the header when a well-known field follows it (header.missing_colon); Python ends the header at that line, so the To field after it is body text.
The same healing: emlkit's body begins after the real empty line, Python's at the colonless line.

emlkit joins the unindented 'boundary="B"' line to the Content-Type field it continues (header.unindented_continuation) and frames the multipart; Python ends the header there, finds no boundary and keeps the multipart as one leaf.

With the charset plugin emlkit decodes 'euc-kr' as code page 949 (UHC), the superset Windows, Outlook and Korean webmail write under that label, so 똠 and 햏 decode; Python's euc_kr codec is KS X 1001 alone and turns each into U+FFFD and a stray letter. emlkit reads the mail as it was meant; the plugin does not report the widening (charset-plugin.md, Limitations).
The bytes agree; the same codec difference in the body: CP949 gives 똠, 햏 and 뷁, Python's KS X 1001 euc_kr four U+FFFD in their place. emlkit's text is the right one.

The RFC 2231 continuation splits the EUC-KR character 최 (C3 D6) between filename*1* and filename*2*. emlkit joins the segments' bytes and decodes them once, with the plugin, giving "제안서_최종.hwp"; Python decodes each segment on its own, so the split character and the next are U+FFFD and a stray ideograph. The charset of the first segment is the charset of the whole value; emlkit is right.

A raw EUC-KR filename in a quoted parameter, on a part whose Content-Type declares charset=euc-kr. emlkit decodes it with that charset through the plugin (mime.parameter_unknown_charset, Recovered): "계약서_초안.hwp"; Python reads raw header bytes as UTF-8 (RFC 6532), which they are not, and gives U+FFFD with accidental letters (༭ from the bytes E0 BC AD). The declared charset is the better reading of such webmail. Part [1], which declares no charset, both leave undecoded, and they agree.

The bytes agree. The body declares no charset and is EUC-KR: emlkit delivers it as read, which is not UTF-8, and Python decodes it as US-ASCII with U+FFFD for each 8-bit byte. Neither reads the Korean; emlkit does with ParseOptions.FallbackCharset (charset.missing). That emlkit reports nothing without a fallback is finding 10 of corpus.md.

The bytes agree: valid UTF-8 HTML, whose own meta tag says utf-8, under charset=euc-kr. Both parsers follow the label, which by the policy of issues #62 and #65 is emlkit's default: the plugin decodes it as CP949 into mojibake and the parse reports charset.declaration_suspect at Info, naming UTF-8 as the other reading; Python's KS X 1001 euc_kr gives other mojibake with 43 U+FFFD. With ParseOptions.RecoverCharsetDeclarations emlkit reads the UTF-8 (Recovered); the harness runs without it. Finding 6 of corpus.md.

emlkit frames the body on the boundary its delimiter lines use when the declared one appears on no line (multipart.boundary_mismatch); Python finds no start boundary and keeps the multipart as one leaf.
emlkit reads an empty multipart body as a container with no part (multipart.empty); Python keeps it as a leaf of zero bytes.

With no closing delimiter emlkit's last part runs to the end of the input and keeps its final line ending (multipart.close_not_found): RFC 2046 gives a CRLF to the delimiter that follows it, and none does. Python drops the final line ending as if one did.
emlkit infers the boundary a multipart without a boundary parameter uses (multipart.boundary_inferred); Python reports NoBoundaryInMultipartDefect and keeps one leaf.
emlkit returns a multipart body with no delimiter line as one part with no header (multipart.start_not_found), so the text is still a body part; Python keeps the multipart as one leaf.
Both read the inner multipart's parts as parts of the outer one. emlkit keeps the inner multipart as a container with no part (multipart.nested_boundary_reused), Python as a leaf of zero bytes.
emlkit reads the cut '--Bound-' at the end of the input as the closing delimiter (multipart.close_truncated); Python finds no close and keeps the cut delimiter in the part's body.

The inner multipart/alternative reuses the outer boundary. emlkit reads the inner parts as parts of the outer multipart, and, finding the inner closing delimiter shared, reads the outer one on past it (multipart.close_shared), so a.pdf is its fourth part; Python ends the outer multipart there and drops a.pdf as epilogue. emlkit keeps the attachment a scanner must see.

As in multipart-reused-boundary: emlkit keeps the inner multipart as a container with no part (multipart.nested_boundary_reused, multipart.empty), Python as a leaf of zero bytes (StartBoundaryNotFoundDefect).

emlkit keeps '=ZZ' as text (cte.qp_invalid_hex), reads '=' and a bare CR as a soft line break (cte.qp_invalid_soft_break) and keeps a final '=' (cte.qp_trailing_equals); Python's binascii.a2b_qp drops the text after the bare-CR soft break up to the next line, losing "break\r\n", and drops the final '='.

Python parses a message/delivery-status as one child per field group, each a header with an empty text/plain body; emlkit keeps the part a leaf of role report, whose field groups Node.ReportFields reads (reports.md).

Python parses every message/* type but delivery-status as an embedded message, so the message/disposition-notification fields become the header of a message with an empty body; emlkit keeps the part a leaf of role report, read with Node.ReportFields (reports.md).

With DescendMessages emlkit reads a text/rfc822-headers part as the header block of an embedded message, its one child with an empty body, so the returned message's fields are header fields again (embedded-messages.md); Python keeps it a text leaf.

The bytes agree. A body that declares no charset is delivered by emlkit as it was read (here valid UTF-8), the 8-bit bytes reported with cte.seven_bit_violation; Python decodes it as US-ASCII and replaces each 8-bit byte with U+FFFD. emlkit guesses a charset only with ParseOptions.FallbackCharset.

The bytes agree. emlkit delivers a body declared UTF-8 that is not UTF-8 as it was read and reports charset.invalid_sequence, so a consumer must validate the text; Python replaces the invalid byte with U+FFFD. emlkit re-decodes such a body only with ParseOptions.FallbackCharset.

With the plugin emlkit decodes 'gb2312' as GBK, as WHATWG and mail clients do, so 喆 decodes; Python's gb2312 codec is GB 2312-80 alone: it replaces 喆 with U+FFFD, loses its place and turns the three characters after it (园科技) into others (丛翱萍) and one more U+FFFD. emlkit reads the mail correctly.

The bytes agree; the same codec difference in the gb2312 body: GBK decodes it whole, Python's GB 2312 gives two U+FFFD and garbles the characters after 喆. emlkit's text is the right one; the GB18030 part [1] agrees.

emlkit reads 'Doe, John <john@example.com>' as one address named "Doe, John" (address.unquoted_comma, MimeKit's AllowUnquotedCommaInAddresses default); Python splits it at the comma into a local-only address "Doe" and "John <john@example.com>". AddressOptions.StrictCommas gives Python's reading.
